digo_source: Pakia (2005) App. III (Uuzi kaha); Pakia (2005) App. VI (Chiganda ulimbo)

teaser.en: Hunters once used the sticky milk of this hairy fig as glue, fixing feathers onto arrow shafts.

summary.en: *Uuzi kaha* is the lowveld fig, a hairy-leaved fig of the bush and forest edge that runs with sticky latex. That latex was used to glue the feathers onto arrows.

about.en: *Uuzi kaha* is a fig tree, and like all figs it bleeds a milky latex when a leaf or twig is broken; in this species the latex flows freely. The leaves and young twigs are covered in soft hairs. The small, rounded figs grow in pairs where the leaves join the twigs.

where.en: It grows in bushland and along forest edges. Its paired figs and hairy leaves set it apart from the other wild figs of the coast.

uses.en: The sticky latex was used to glue feathers onto arrow shafts, a small but essential job in making arrows that fly straight.

names.en: Pakia records two Digo names: *uuzi kaha*, and *chiganda ulimbo*, which is shared with Duruma and means 'fig with latex' (*ulimbo* is sticky latex or birdlime). In English it is the lowveld fig. Swahili uses the general fig name *mkuyu*, which in Digo belongs to the Cape fig (*Ficus sur*).

reason.en: Rubber vine, another plant valued for its latex

sources: Pakia, M. (2005) African Traditional Plant Knowledge Today: an ethnobotanical study of the Digo at the Kenya Coast. PhD thesis, Univ. Bayreuth, Appendix III (Digo–botanical name list) & Appendix VI (name semantics). https://epub.uni-bayreuth.de/881/1/Pakia.pdf
